newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major set to announce May 1 as election date.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major set to announce May 1 as election date.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major looked set to announce on Monday that Britain would go to the polls on May 1, officially launching an election battle which the opposition Labour party is overwhelmingly favoured to win.
Virtually every newspaper said Major would end months of speculation by telling the cabinet of his decision before going to Buckingham Palace to ask Queen Elizabeth to formally dissolve parliament.

Major, whose Conservative party trails badly in opinion polls, would begin his campaign immediately with a series of media interviews before starting a series of trips to key parliamentary constituencies across the country, the papers said.

The election date seemed more certain than the timing of the announcement, since Major has made little secret of his wish to hold the poll on May 1 and try to secure an unprecedented fifth consecutive term for the Conservatives.

Home Secretary (interior minister) Michael Howard apparently confirmed the date in an interview on BBC Radio on Sunday. "On May 2 it's perfectly clear that one of two men are likely, could be, prime minister of this country," he said.

Howard was referring to Major and Tony Blair, whose Labour party is around 25 points ahead in the polls and poised to win its first election since 1974. No British party has overturned such a large opinion poll deficit so close to an election.

Blair, who has transformed Labour's fortunes by moving it towards the political centre, wrote an article for Monday's Sun tabloid newspaper in which he repeated promises that the party would be tough with its European Union partners.

Although the Conservatives are deeply split over policy towards the EU, Major has continually claimed that a Labour government would sell the country out to Brussels and willingly help to build a federal superstate.
Blair rejected the accusation, saying that as a British patriot he would fight for the country's interests.
It was no coincidence that he was writing in the best-selling Sun, whose readers have in the past mainly voted for the Conservatives.
"Blair looks at the (Conservative) record on Europe and says: We can do better than this.' In truth, it would be hard to do any worse," the paper said in an editorial.

To try to improve his party's chances, Major has accepted a Blair challenge to take part in televised debates. Blair has never held ministerial office and Major's advisers say he believes he can exploit this inexperience.

The minority Liberal Democrat party immediately threatened legal action to block the debates, saying rules on political impartiality during campaigns meant their leader Paddy Ashdown had to be included in such broadcasts.
British election campaigns usually take around three weeks, but if Major declades May 1 as polling day the pre-electoral battle will last for 45 days, the longest for more than 80 years.
